title: Test-Time Scaling of Text-to-Image Flow Matching Models with Noise-Rejuvenated Sequential Monte Carlo

paper.title: Test-Time Scaling of Text-to-Image Flow Matching Models with Noise-Rejuvenated Sequential Monte Carlo
paper.abstract: Abstract Test-time scaling of diffusion models with sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) has become a promising strategy for sampling under user-specified rewards, such as human preference scores. However, the standard SMC framework typically relies on stochastic proposals and therefore does not directly transfer to flow matching models, in which inference is governed by deterministic ODEs. In this work, we introduce noise-rejuvenated SMC, an inference-time scaling method tailored for text-to-image flow matching models. Our key idea is to perturb each resampled particle by changing its source noise and constructing a new intermediate state using its current endpoint estimate. This moves the particle to another state that remains representable under the flow-matching interpolation form, enabling particle exploration without converting the sampler to an SDE. We further introduce a look-ahead mechanism to refine resampled particles before weighting. Experiments on Stable Diffusion 3, FLUX.1-dev, and Z-Image demonstrate consistent improvements in reward-guided generation, while ablation studies validate the contributions of noise rejuvenation and look-ahead refinement. Code is available at https://github.com/shermanlian/NR-SMC .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Inference-time scaling of diffusion models has shown promising results by tilting the stochastic generation towards user-specified target distributions ( Ben-Hamu et al., 2024 ; Eyring et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Singhal et al., 2025 ) using explicitly defined reward signals such as the CLIP-score ( Radford et al., 2021 ) and human preference scores ( Xu et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2023b , HPS,) . Despite their strong performance, many prior methods ( Ben-Hamu et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Qi et al., 2024 ) require backpropagating reward gradients during inference and therefore assume differentiable reward functions. This increases inference cost and limits their applicability to large-scale models and complex or black-box reward signals. Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) methods offer a natural alternative by using reward evaluations only for reweighting and resampling particles, rather than for gradient-based optimization ( Wu et al., 2023a ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Zhao, 2026 ; Singhal et al., 2025 ) . As a result, SMC can guide diffusion sampling without differentiating through the reward function or performing test-time training. By maintaining multiple trajectories, SMC enables exploration and progressively twists the sampling process toward regions with higher user-specified rewards ( Singhal et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) . At the same time, standard SMC algorithms rely on stochastic sampling processes, and are therefore not directly applicable to flow matching (FM) models ( Lipman et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) , , which have become an important class of generative models. Figure 1 : Qualitative comparison between vanilla sampling and our method on text-to-image generation using Stable Diffusion 3 (SD3) ( Esser et al., 2024 ) , FLUX.1 ( Labs et al., 2025 ) , and Z-Image ( Team, 2025 ) . Our method steers generation toward higher reward objectives, producing outputs that better align with the input prompts without additional training or gradient computation. To obtain the stochastic transitions needed by SMC in deterministic FM samplers, a straightforward baseline is to perturb particle states directly, for example by injecting noise at each solver step. While this does introduce additional stochasticity, it also deviates from the flow matching ODE-based integration path: z 1 = z 0 + ∫ 0 1 v θ ​ ( z t , t ) ​ 𝑑 t , z_{1}=z_{0}+\int_{0}^{1}v_{\theta}(z_{t},t)dt, (1) where z 0 z_{0} and z 1 z_{1} denote the source and target samples, respectively, and v θ ​ ( z t , t ) = d ​ z t / d ​ t v_{\theta}(z_{t},t)={dz_{t}}/{dt} is the learned velocity field ( Liu et al., 2022 ) . In this scenario, adding noise to Equation 1 often degrades the generation quality and requires more sampling steps for denoising ( Liu et al., 2022 ) . As a consequence, most existing SMC approaches fail to improve the results in flow matching models, since they do not generate new paths. To address this issue, we introduce noise-rejuvenated SMC, a resampling-time perturbation strategy for ODE-based flow matching samplers. Our method keeps the original flow matching solver for normal propagation and injects stochasticity only when particles are resampled. Specifically, after computing the current endpoint estimate from the current particle, we replace its source noise with newly sampled Gaussian noise and construct a rejuvenated intermediate state using the flow-matching interpolation parameterization. The resulting state is subsequently propagated using the original flow-matching solver. This operation constructs an alternative intermediate state compatible with the flow-matching interpolation parameterization, providing controlled exploration while avoiding the quality degradation caused by injecting noise at every solver step. We further introduce a look-ahead mechanism that refines the rejuvenated particles with an additional flow-matching update, leading to more informative resampling decisions. We evaluate our approach on several state-of-the-art flow matching text-to-image models, including Stable Diffusion 3 (SD3) ( Esser et al., 2024 ) , Flux.1 ( Labs et al., 2025 ) , and Z-Image ( Team, 2025 ) . The results show that our method effectively steers generation toward user-specified reward objectives at inference time, without requiring additional training or gradient-based optimization. Figure 1 illustrates representative examples comparing vanilla sampling and our approach. In summary, our contributions are as follows: • We present a novel inference-time scaling method for flow matching based on sequential Monte Carlo. Our method enables particle exploration for diversity while preserving generation fidelity. • We introduce a resampling-time perturbation strategy, referred to as noise rejuvenation, which introduces stochasticity over the ODE path and thus unleashes the potential of SMC for flow matching applications. • We integrate a look-ahead mechanism allowing for further refinement of the resampled particles. • We empirically show that our proposed method is effective across various state-of-the-art text-to-image flow matching models.

sections.heading: 2.1 Diffusion Models
sections.text: Diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ) , in the context of generative modeling, constitute a forward noising process and a reverse process for new data sampling. Its reverse-time process is given by ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ) d z t = [ f ( z t , t ) − g ( t ) 2 ∇ log p t ( z t ) ] d t + g ( t ) d w ¯ t , dz_{t}=[f(z_{t},t)-g(t)^{2}\nabla\log p_{t}(z_{t})]dt+g(t)d\bar{w}_{t}, (3) where ∇ log ⁡ p t ​ ( z ) \nabla\log p_{t}(z) is the score function and w ¯ t \bar{w}_{t} is a reverse-time Wiener process.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: In this work, we consider flow matching in the latent space for conditional image generation. Specifically, let us denote the image by x x and adopt a decoder x = D ϕ ​ ( z ) x=D_{\phi}(z) through e.g., a variational auto-encoder ( Kingma & Welling, 2013 ; Rombach et al., 2022 , VAE,) with pretrained parameters ϕ \phi . sections.heading: 3.2 Noise Rejuvenation for Flow Matching
sections.text: Figure 2 : Illustration of flow matching using standard SMC (left) and our noise-rejuvenated SMC (right) during inference-time sampling. For clarity, we only visualize two particles (purple). When directly applying SMC to flow matching models, resampling leads to particle collapse, producing identical trajectories and final outputs (left). In contrast, noise rejuvenation injects controlled stochasticity during resampling, inducing occasional “jumps” that allow particles to escape collapsed trajectories and explore alternative paths throughout the sampling process (right). While flow matching employs ODE solvers as the default choice for high-quality data generation, the resulting deterministic dynamics are not directly compatible with traditional SMC methods, which rely on stochastic transitions to maintain particle diversity during sampling. See Figure 2 for an illustration. One possible remedy is to convert the FM sampler into an SDE or inject state noise at every solver step. We avoid this approach because it replaces the default ODE inference path with a globally stochastic sampler, introduces an additional noise schedule, and injects randomness even when no resampling-induced collapse occurs. Such global stochasticity may move particles away from the learned FM integration path and degrade generation fidelity. We instead introduce noise rejuvenation, which injects stochasticity only at resampling steps to mitigate particle collapse while largely retaining the behavior of the underlying ODE sampler. sections.heading: 3.3 Look-ahead Refinement
sections.text: Noise rejuvenation changes the particle state immediately after resampling, as illustrated in Figure 2 (right). Although this operation preserves particle diversity, the reward evaluated immediately after rejuvenation may be less reliable because the perturbed particle has not yet been propagated by the flow matching dynamics. To obtain a more informative and stable estimate for particle selection, we introduce a one-step look-ahead refinement. Concretely, after the noise rejuvenation produces a perturbed state z ~ t \tilde{z}_{t} , we apply one additional deterministic flow matching update z ~ t + Δ ​ t LA = z ~ t + Δ ​ t ⋅ v θ ​ ( z ~ t , t , c ) , \tilde{z}_{t+\Delta t}^{\mathrm{LA}}=\tilde{z}_{t}+\Delta t\cdot v_{\theta}(\tilde{z}_{t},t,c), (18) where Δ ​ t \Delta t is the solver step size. We utilize Equation 10 to estimate the corresponding terminal latent from this look-ahead state as z ^ 1 , t LA = z ~ t + Δ ​ t LA + ( 1 − t − Δ ​ t ) ​ v θ ​ ( z ~ t + Δ ​ t LA , t + Δ ​ t , c ) . \hat{z}_{1,t}^{\mathrm{LA}}=\tilde{z}_{t+\Delta t}^{\mathrm{LA}}+(1-t-\Delta t)v_{\theta}(\tilde{z}_{t+\Delta t}^{\mathrm{LA}},t+\Delta t,c). (19) We then compute its reward r t LA r_{t}^{\mathrm{LA}} and define a look-ahead potential according to G t LA ( z 0 : t , c ) = exp ( λ max [ { r ¯ ( z s , c ) } s = 0 t , r t LA ] ) . G_{t}^{\mathrm{LA}}(z_{0:t},c)=\exp\left(\lambda\max\left[\{\bar{r}(z_{s},c)\}_{s=0}^{t},r_{t}^{\mathrm{LA}}\right]\right). (20) This potential evaluates each rejuvenated particle after a short roll-out under the same flow matching dynamics. Therefore, resampling is guided not only by the current perturbed state, but also by an estimate of how the particle will evolve in the next step. From the perspective of SMC, this can be viewed as an auxiliary potential that approximates the future contribution of each particle to the terminal reward, leading to more stable and informative particle selection.

sections.heading: 4 Related Work
sections.text: Recent studies in text-to-image generation have shown that prompt adherence is a key challenge for diffusion-based models ( Xu et al., 2023 ; Chefer et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024b ; Feng et al., 2022 ; Feng et al., 2023 ) , for example, missing objects, incorrectly bound attributes, and wrong locations ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) . Here, we focus on addressing these problems using inference-time scaling techniques, such as gradient-based optimization ( Clark et al., 2023 ; Prabhudesai et al., 2023 ) and gradient-free guidance ( Kim et al., 2025b ; Jain et al., 2025 ) . Particularly, gradient-free methods based on SMC have drawn increasing attention since they require less computation and alleviate over-optimization ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Singhal et al., 2025 ) . SMC ( Doucet et al., 2001 ; Naesseth et al., 2019 ) has emerged as a versatile framework for probabilistic modelling, providing effective tools for sampling and inference ( Johansen, 2009 ; Ryan et al., 2016 ; Hol et al., 2006 ; Lindsten et al., 2014 ) . More recently, SMC has been applied to autoregressive ( Zhao et al., 2024 ; Loula et al., 2025 ; Dang et al., 2025 ) and diffusion models ( Jasra & Doucet, 2009 ; Kim et al., 2025a ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024a ; Skreta et al., 2025 ) as a powerful sampler capable of drawing data from user-preferred distributions. In particular, SMC methods can be perfectly integrated into the inference of pretrained diffusion models, in which external reward signals, such as CLIP scores ( Radford et al., 2021 ) and Human preference scores ( Wu et al., 2023b ; Xu et al., 2023 ) , are used to guide the diffusion process towards high-reward target areas. Singhal et al. (2025) formulate this as a Feynman-Kac interacting particle system. Subsequent methods further introduce alternative sampling strategies, such as Gibbs sampling or importance sampling, to improve particle diversity and efficiency ( Ou et al., 2025 ; Dang et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) . However, these methods are primarily designed for stochastic diffusion models and rely on stochastic proposals or SDE-based sampling dynamics.

sections.heading: Benchmarks and metrics.
sections.text: Following Singhal et al. (2025) and Esser et al. (2024) , we evaluate our method on GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) and T2I-CompBench ( Huang et al., 2023 ) . For GenEval, we report the overall and task-wise accuracy together with ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) , Human Preference Score v2 (HPSv2) ( Wu et al., 2023b ) , and Correct Image rate ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) . For T2I-CompBench, we report BVQA, ImageReward, and HPSv2. All metrics are computed using their official implementations with default settings. ImageReward is used as the reward function for particle weighting and resampling, while all other metrics are used only for evaluation.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We evaluate our method on three text-to-image flow matching backbones: Stable Diffusion 3 (SD3) ( Esser et al., 2024 ) , FLUX.1-dev ( Labs et al., 2025 ) , and Z-Image ( Team, 2025 ) . For each backbone, we compare the original deterministic inference pipeline, FK-Diffusion ( Singhal et al., 2025 ) , and our noise-rejuvenated SMC. We also compare with other text-to-image models, including minDALL-E ( Ramesh et al., 2022 ) , Stable Diffusion v1.5 (SD v1.5) ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , PixArt- α \alpha ( Chen et al., 2023 ) , Stable Diffusion v2.1 (SD v2.1) ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , DALL-E 2 ( Ramesh et al., 2022 ) , SDXL ( Podell et al., 2023 ) , SDXL Turbo ( Podell et al., 2023 ) , IF-XL ( Saharia et al., 2022 ) , and DALL-E 3 ( Betker et al., 2023 ) .

sections.heading: Implementation details.
sections.text: For all experiments, the number of inference steps is set to 50. For SMC-based methods, we use N = 4 N=4 particles and apply resampling every 5 steps within the window from step 5 to step 35. For the original deterministic pipeline, we generate 4 independent samples with different noise initializations to match the number of generated candidates used by SMC-based methods. The guidance strength is set to λ = 10.0 \lambda=10.0 . Unless otherwise stated, our method uses the look-ahead refinement described in Section 3.3 .

sections.heading: Evaluation protocol.
sections.text: For each prompt, our method produces N N final particles. We decode and evaluate each particle independently, and report the average of each evaluation metric over all particles and prompts. We apply the same protocol to the corresponding vanilla pipeline by generating N N independent samples. sections.heading: GenEval evaluation.
sections.text: The main quantitative results on GenEval are summarized in Table 1 . Across all three flow-matching backbones, our method consistently improves over the original deterministic inference pipeline. On SD3 ( Esser et al., 2024 ) , noise-rejuvenated SMC improves the GenEval score from 0.718 0.718 to 0.748 0.748 and the ImageReward score from 1.081 1.081 to 1.268 1.268 . On FLUX.1-dev ( Labs et al., 2025 ) , our method improves ImageReward from 0.986 0.986 to 1.218 1.218 , while also improving GenEval and HPSv2. On Z-Image ( Team, 2025 ) , our method improves GenEval from 0.756 0.756 to 0.775 0.775 and ImageReward from 0.810 0.810 to 0.977 0.977 . In contrast, FK-Diffusion ( Singhal et al., 2025 ) consistently degrades GenEval and Correct Image across these backbones, suggesting that SMC methods designed for stochastic diffusion samplers do not directly transfer to deterministic flow-matching inference. We further report the task-wise GenEval results in Table 2 . Our method achieves improved or comparable accuracy across most categories, with particularly clear gains on two-object generation, counting, and position. These categories require object-level compositional alignment and are sensitive to missing objects or incorrect spatial relations. The improvements on GenEval, HPSv2, and Correct Image are especially important because these metrics are used only for evaluation and not for particle weighting or resampling.

sections.heading: T2I-CompBench evaluation.
sections.text: We additionally evaluate compositional generation on T2I-CompBench in Table 3 . Across color, shape, and texture composition, our method improves most metrics on SD3, FLUX.1-dev, and Z-Image. In particular, the improvements on BVQA and HPSv2 provide evidence beyond the ImageReward guidance signal. These results suggest that noise-rejuvenated SMC improves reward-guided generation while also transferring to broader compositional evaluation settings.

sections.heading: Qualitative results.
sections.text: Qualitative comparisons are shown in Figure 3 and Figure 4 . We compare samples generated by the original SD3 and FLUX.1-dev pipelines, FK-Diffusion, and our method under the same prompts. FK-Diffusion introduces additional stochasticity but can produce artifacts or reduce image consistency when directly applied to flow-matching samplers. For example, it may produce incorrect object counts or unnatural textures, such as the banana example with SD3 and the teddy-bear example with FLUX. In contrast, our method tends to better follow the prompts in terms of object counts, color attributes, and spatial composition, while preserving visual quality. sections.heading: Effect of noise rejuvenation.
sections.text: Directly applying SMC to deterministic flow matching leads to particle collapse after resampling, causing all particles to follow the same trajectory and converge to identical samples, as illustrated in Figure 5 . Noise rejuvenation alleviates this issue by introducing stochasticity only during resampling, preserving particle diversity and enabling exploration along distinct trajectories. To isolate the effect of noise rejuvenation, we apply it to the original SD3 pipeline without SMC. As shown in Table 4 , noise rejuvenation only slightly affects generation performance, suggesting that the introduced approximation errors are limited and the underlying flow matching behavior is largely preserved. In contrast, injecting noise at every sampling step through an SDE solver significantly degrades generation quality (Figure 6 ). These results suggest that, in this setting, stochasticity is beneficial only when introduced selectively, rather than throughout the entire sampling process. sections.text: We evaluate the effect of the look-ahead mechanism in Table 5 . sections.heading: Effect of guidance strength.
sections.text: We examine the effect of the guidance strength λ \lambda in our framework by varying its value at inference time while keeping all other components fixed. As shown in Figure 8 , when λ = 0 \lambda=0 , corresponding to the absence of guidance, all evaluation metrics attain their lowest values. The performance improves steadily as λ \lambda increases from 0 to 10, suggesting that setting a suitable guidance strength such as λ = 10 \lambda=10 effectively biases the sampling process toward higher-reward regions of the data distribution. We also observe that increasing λ \lambda to 20 induces higher resampling probability but gives marginal performance gains and reduces sample diversity, as illustrated in Figure 7 . Overall, these results indicate that moderate guidance strengths are sufficient to achieve strong performance in practice. sections.heading: Effect of resampling frequency.
sections.text: We investigate whether the model benefits from more frequent resampling by varying the resampling interval f f while keeping the total number of solver steps fixed. As shown in Figure 9 , the effect of resampling frequency illustrates diminishing returns: ImageReward improves as resampling becomes less frequent and quickly saturates around f = 5 f=5 , while Human Preference score shows only minor variation across different frequencies. These results indicate that our method does not require frequent resampling to perform well and remains robust under reduced inference-time budgets.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We propose noise rejuvenation, a resampling-time perturbation strategy for applying SMC to deterministic flow-matching text-to-image samplers. By replacing the source noise of a resampled particle using its fixed pre-rejuvenation endpoint estimate, our method restores particle exploration without switching the entire sampler to an SDE. We further introduce a look-ahead refinement mechanism for more informative particle selection. Experiments on SD3, FLUX.1-dev, and Z-Image show consistent improvements over vanilla sampling and FK-Diffusion across GenEval, T2I-CompBench, and human-aligned reward metrics.

sections.heading: Limitations and future work.
sections.text: Our method requires additional inference cost that grows approximately linearly with the number of particles. Moreover, noise rejuvenation relies on an approximate endpoint estimate and therefore does not guarantee exact preservation of the original terminal distribution. Strong reward guidance may also introduce local artifacts for challenging compositional prompts. Future work will explore more efficient resampling strategies, adaptive reward schedules, and invariant rejuvenation mechanisms that are more tightly coupled with deterministic flow-matching samplers.

sections.heading: Broader Impact Statement
sections.text: The proposed framework enables reward-guided test-time scaling for flow-matching text-to-image models without requiring model fine-tuning. Its compatibility with black-box reward functions makes it applicable to a broad range of reward-guided generation tasks. The main limitation is the increased inference cost due to multiple particles and look-ahead refinement. As particle weights and resampling decisions are determined by an external reward model, the generated samples may inherit its biases. Strong reward guidance can further amplify these biases, reduce sample diversity, and concentrate particles on a small set of high-reward outputs. The choice of reward model and guidance strength should therefore be made with care.

sections.text: Given an intermediate state z t z_{t} and a marginal velocity field v ∗ v^{\ast} , the corresponding ODE endpoint is obtained by integrating the velocity field along the remaining trajectory: z 1 ODE = z t + ∫ t 1 v ∗ ​ ( z s , s , c ) ​ 𝑑 s . z_{1}^{\mathrm{ODE}}=z_{t}+\int_{t}^{1}v^{\ast}(z_{s},s,c)\,ds. (22) For a particular pair ( z 0 , z 1 ) (z_{0},z_{1}) , differentiating this interpolation gives the conditional velocity u t ​ ( z t ∣ z 0 , z 1 ) = d ​ z t d ​ t = z 1 − z 0 . u_{t}(z_{t}\mid z_{0},z_{1})=\frac{dz_{t}}{dt}=z_{1}-z_{0}. (23) Importantly, this pairwise conditional velocity is different from the marginal velocity field used during inference. Under the standard flow-matching objective, the optimal marginal velocity is v ∗ ( z t , t , c ) = 𝔼 [ z 1 − z 0 ∣ z t , c ] . v^{\ast}(z_{t},t,c)=\mathbb{E}\left[z_{1}-z_{0}\mid z_{t},c\right]. (24) Note that Equation 22 also gives z 1 = z t + ( 1 − t ) ​ ( z 1 − z 0 ) z_{1}=z_{t}+(1-t)(z_{1}-z_{0}) . Taking the conditional expectation of this identity given ( z t , c ) (z_{t},c) yields z t + ( 1 − t ) v ∗ ( z t , t , c ) = 𝔼 [ z 1 ∣ z t , c ] . z_{t}+(1-t)v^{\ast}(z_{t},t,c)=\mathbb{E}\left[z_{1}\mid z_{t},c\right]. In general, z ^ 1 \hat{z}_{1} should be interpreted as an endpoint estimate rather than an exact sample-wise reconstruction. Its error arises from both the conditional uncertainty of z 1 z_{1} given ( z t , c ) (z_{t},c) and the approximation error of the learned velocity field. Exact reconstruction requires stronger conditions, such as a uniquely determined conditional endpoint and an exact learned velocity field. Therefore, holding z ^ 1 \hat{z}_{1} fixed during the local rejuvenation update does not by itself establish equality between the rejuvenated and original terminal marginals, consistent with the formulation in Section 3 .

sections.heading: Appendix B Ablation Study: Resampling at Different Stages
sections.text: We investigate how the timing of resampling along the flow matching trajectory affects performance. Specifically, we fix the length of the resampling window (i.e., t end − t start t_{\text{end}}-t_{\text{start}} ) and vary its position to cover early, middle, and late stages of the trajectory. Results in Table 11 show that performance is relatively robust to these choices, while resampling at very late stages tends to be less effective, with mid-range windows achieving slightly better results. One possible explanation is that, at very late stages, particles are already close to high-reward regions and exploration is largely exhausted. As a result, injecting noise at this stage may mainly introduce additional perturbations without promoting further exploration. sections.heading: Appendix D Analysis of Local-Perturbation Rejuvenation
sections.text: To better understand the role of the rejuvenation mechanism, we include a diagnostic comparison with directly perturbing the intermediate particle states in the flow matching pipeline. Specifically, let { z t i } i = 1 K \{z_{t}^{i}\}_{i=1}^{K} denote the resampled particles at time t t . The local perturbation strategy updates each particle independently as z ~ t i = z t i + σ t ​ ϵ i , ϵ i ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) . \tilde{z}_{t}^{i}=z_{t}^{i}+\sigma_{t}\epsilon^{i},\qquad\epsilon^{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I). (27) where σ t \sigma_{t} controls the noise magnitude. The look-ahead step mentioned in Section 3.3 is then applied to propagate the perturbed particles forward along the deterministic flow matching dynamics. In other words, we add noise to Equation 7 to construct a corresponding SDE of the form z t + 1 = z t + ∫ t t + 1 v θ ​ ( z t , t , c ) ​ 𝑑 t + σ t ​ d ​ W t , z_{t+1}=z_{t}+\int_{t}^{t+1}v_{\theta}(z_{t},t,c)dt\;+\;\sigma_{t}dW_{t}, (28) where W W is a Wiener process. While this creates a dynamic trajectory, its effectiveness is highly sensitive to the choice of σ t \sigma_{t} and the resampling stage. When σ t \sigma_{t} is small, the perturbations are quickly damped by the deterministic flow dynamics, leading to rapid particle collapse. Conversely, large perturbations may significantly degrade sample quality, even with the look-ahead refinement. The performance of different σ t \sigma_{t} used in this strategy is summarized in Table 13 . These observations motivate our initial-noise rejuvenation strategy, which perturbs the initial noise and propagates the resulting variation to the intermediate state z t z_{t} through the linear interpolation structure of flow matching. As shown in Table 13 , our strategy provides a better overall trade-off across GenEval, ImageReward, and HPSv2, supporting its use as the default rejuvenation mechanism in our framework.

Schön thomas.schon@uu.se Affiliation: Department of Information Technology Affiliation: Uppsala University, Sweden Abstract Test-time scaling of diffusion models with sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) has become a promising strategy for sampling under user-specified rewards, such as human preference scores. However, the standard SMC framework typically relies on stochastic proposals and therefore does not directly transfer to flow matching models, in which inference is governed by deterministic ODEs. In this work, we introduce noise-rejuvenated SMC, an inference-time scaling method tailored for text-to-image flow matching models. Our key idea is to perturb each resampled particle by changing its source noise and constructing a new intermediate state using its current endpoint estimate. This moves the particle to another state that remains representable under the flow-matching interpolation form, enabling particle exploration without converting the sampler to an SDE. We further introduce a look-ahead mechanism to refine resampled particles before weighting. Experiments on Stable Diffusion 3, FLUX.1-dev, and Z-Image demonstrate consistent improvements in reward-guided generation, while ablation studies validate the contributions of noise rejuvenation and look-ahead refinement. Code is available at https://github.com/shermanlian/NR-SMC . 1 Introduction Inference-time scaling of diffusion models has shown promising results by tilting the stochastic generation towards user-specified target distributions ( Ben-Hamu et al., 2024 ; Eyring et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Singhal et al., 2025 ) using explicitly defined reward signals such as the CLIP-score ( Radford et al., 2021 ) and human preference scores ( Xu et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2023b , HPS,) . Despite their strong performance, many prior methods ( Ben-Hamu et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Qi et al., 2024 ) require backpropagating reward gradients during inference and therefore assume differentiable reward functions. This increases inference cost and limits their applicability to large-scale models and complex or black-box reward signals. Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) methods offer a natural alternative by using reward evaluations only for reweighting and resampling particles, rather than for gradient-based optimization ( Wu et al., 2023a ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Zhao, 2026 ; Singhal et al., 2025 ) . As a result, SMC can guide diffusion sampling without differentiating through the reward function or performing test-time training. By maintaining multiple trajectories, SMC enables exploration and progressively twists the sampling process toward regions with higher user-specified rewards ( Singhal et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) . At the same time, standard SMC algorithms rely on stochastic sampling processes, and are therefore not directly applicable to flow matching (FM) models ( Lipman et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) , , which have become an important class of generative models. Figure 1 : Qualitative comparison between vanilla sampling and our method on text-to-image generation using Stable Diffusion 3 (SD3) ( Esser et al., 2024 ) , FLUX.1 ( Labs et al., 2025 ) , and Z-Image ( Team, 2025 ) . Our method steers generation toward higher reward objectives, producing outputs that better align with the input prompts without additional training or gradient computation. To obtain the stochastic transitions needed by SMC in deterministic FM samplers, a straightforward baseline is to perturb particle states directly, for example by injecting noise at each solver step. While this does introduce additional stochasticity, it also deviates from the flow matching ODE-based integration path: z 1 = z 0 + ∫ 0 1 v θ ​ ( z t , t ) ​ 𝑑 t , z_{1}=z_{0}+\int_{0}^{1}v_{\theta}(z_{t},t)dt, (1) where z 0 z_{0} and z 1 z_{1} denote the source and target samples, respectively, and v θ ​ ( z t , t ) = d ​ z t / d ​ t v_{\theta}(z_{t},t)={dz_{t}}/{dt} is the learned velocity field ( Liu et al., 2022 ) . In this scenario, adding noise to Equation 1 often degrades the generation quality and requires more sampling steps for denoising ( Liu et al., 2022 ) . As a consequence, most existing SMC approaches fail to improve the results in flow matching models, since they do not generate new paths. To address this issue, we introduce noise-rejuvenated SMC, a resampling-time perturbation strategy for ODE-based flow matching samplers. Our method keeps the original flow matching solver for normal propagation and injects stochasticity only when particles are resampled. Specifically, after computing the current endpoint estimate from the current particle, we replace its source noise with newly sampled Gaussian noise and construct a rejuvenated intermediate state using the flow-matching interpolation parameterization. The resulting state is subsequently propagated using the original flow-matching solver. This operation constructs an alternative intermediate state compatible with the flow-matching interpolation parameterization, providing controlled exploration while avoiding the quality degradation caused by injecting noise at every solver step. We further introduce a look-ahead mechanism that refines the rejuvenated particles with an additional flow-matching update, leading to more informative resampling decisions. We evaluate our approach on several state-of-the-art flow matching text-to-image models, including Stable Diffusion 3 (SD3) ( Esser et al., 2024 ) , Flux.1 ( Labs et al., 2025 ) , and Z-Image ( Team, 2025 ) . The results show that our method effectively steers generation toward user-specified reward objectives at inference time, without requiring additional training or gradient-based optimization. Figure 1 illustrates representative examples comparing vanilla sampling and our approach. In summary, our contributions are as follows: • We present a novel inference-time scaling method for flow matching based on sequential Monte Carlo. Our method enables particle exploration for diversity while preserving generation fidelity. • We introduce a resampling-time perturbation strategy, referred to as noise rejuvenation, which introduces stochasticity over the ODE path and thus unleashes the potential of SMC for flow matching applications. • We integrate a look-ahead mechanism allowing for further refinement of the resampled particles. • We empirically show that our proposed method is effective across various state-of-the-art text-to-image flow matching models. 2 Background 2.1 Diffusion Models Diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ) , in the context of generative modeling, constitute a forward noising process and a reverse process for new data sampling. Specifically, diffusion models can be characterized by the following forward-time stochastic differential equation (SDE): d ​ z t = f ⁡ ( z t , t ) ​ d ​ t + g ⁡ ( t ) ​ d ​ w t , dz_{t}=f(z_{t},t)dt+g(t)dw_{t}, (2) where f f is the drift function, g g is the diffusion function, and w t w_{t} is a standard Wiener process. Specifically, let us denote the image by x x and adopt a decoder x = D ϕ ​ ( z ) x=D_{\phi}(z) through e.g., a variational auto-encoder ( Kingma & Welling, 2013 ; Rombach et al., 2022 , VAE,) with pretrained parameters ϕ \phi . During inference, sampling starts from an initial Gaussian noise z 0 z_{0} and follows the learned ODE dynamics toward the final latent state z 1 z_{1} at t = 1 t=1 . The final image is then obtained by decoding the final z 1 z_{1} as x = D ϕ ​ ( z 1 ) x=D_{\phi}(z_{1}) . 3.1 Reward-Guided Conditional Distribution One way to steer prompt-conditional generation is to reward-tilt the pretrained conditional distribution under a fixed prompt. Throughout this section, c c denotes the same text prompt used by both the flow-matching sampler and the reward model: the velocity field v θ ​ ( z t , t , c ) v_{\theta}(z_{t},t,c) induces the base prompt-conditional distribution p θ ​ ( z 1 ∣ c ) p_{\theta}(z_{1}\mid c) , while r ⁡ ( x , c ) r(x,c) is an external scalar score that evaluates the decoded image x x under the same prompt. When directly applying SMC to flow matching models, resampling leads to particle collapse, producing identical trajectories and final outputs (left). While flow matching employs ODE solvers as the default choice for high-quality data generation, the resulting deterministic dynamics are not directly compatible with traditional SMC methods, which rely on stochastic transitions to maintain particle diversity during sampling. Here, we focus on addressing these problems using inference-time scaling techniques, such as gradient-based optimization ( Clark et al., 2023 ; Prabhudesai et al., 2023 ) and gradient-free guidance ( Kim et al., 2025b ; Jain et al., 2025 ) . Particularly, gradient-free methods based on SMC have drawn increasing attention since they require less computation and alleviate over-optimization ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Singhal et al., 2025 ) . SMC ( Doucet et al., 2001 ; Naesseth et al., 2019 ) has emerged as a versatile framework for probabilistic modelling, providing effective tools for sampling and inference ( Johansen, 2009 ; Ryan et al., 2016 ; Hol et al., 2006 ; Lindsten et al., 2014 ) . More recently, SMC has been applied to autoregressive ( Zhao et al., 2024 ; Loula et al., 2025 ; Dang et al., 2025 ) and diffusion models ( Jasra & Doucet, 2009 ; Kim et al., 2025a ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024a ; Skreta et al., 2025 ) as a powerful sampler capable of drawing data from user-preferred distributions. In particular, SMC methods can be perfectly integrated into the inference of pretrained diffusion models, in which external reward signals, such as CLIP scores ( Radford et al., 2021 ) and Human preference scores ( Wu et al., 2023b ; Xu et al., 2023 ) , are used to guide the diffusion process towards high-reward target areas. Singhal et al. (2025) formulate this as a Feynman-Kac interacting particle system. Subsequent methods further introduce alternative sampling strategies, such as Gibbs sampling or importance sampling, to improve particle diversity and efficiency ( Ou et al., 2025 ; Dang et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) . Directly applying SMC to deterministic flow matching leads to particle collapse after resampling, causing all particles to follow the same trajectory and converge to identical samples, as illustrated in Figure 5 . Noise rejuvenation alleviates this issue by introducing stochasticity only during resampling, preserving particle diversity and enabling exploration along distinct trajectories. To isolate the effect of noise rejuvenation, we apply it to the original SD3 pipeline without SMC. As shown in Table 4 , noise rejuvenation only slightly affects generation performance, suggesting that the introduced approximation errors are limited and the underlying flow matching behavior is largely preserved. In contrast, injecting noise at every sampling step through an SDE solver significantly degrades generation quality (Figure 6 ). These results suggest that, in this setting, stochasticity is beneficial only when introduced selectively, rather than throughout the entire sampling process.
